Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

1

sion which is expensive, and so instead the gradient can be calculated over the squared l2 norm of
the output. Putting this together, we arrive at the final importance estimation equation:

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

A A PPENDIX

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.

1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

1

over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

meaning this is only calculated once, and then the train-set may be discarded after. We replace

of the gradient. For multi-dimensional outputs, this gradient must be calculated over every dimen-

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

A A PPENDIX

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.

Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

synthesis.contribution_summary: This Tiny Paper proposes LFSSD, an extension of Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) for machine unlearning. It replaces SSD's Fisher-information-diagonal importance estimate with the gradient of the l2 norm of the model output, the sensitivity measure of Aljundi et al. (2018). As a result, forgetting needs neither retraining nor labels for the forget samples. The method is evaluated against SSD and other baselines on class, subclass, and face-unlearning tasks with ResNet and ViT models.
synthesis.originality: The contribution is combinational. The authors credit the dampening rule to SSD and the importance estimator to Aljundi et al. (2018). The new element is pairing them so that unlearning becomes label-free. This framing is honest, and the scope is appropriate for a tiny paper, but the contribution is incremental rather than a new algorithm. The paper hedges its claim to be the first retraining-free method needing only unlabelled forget samples in the introduction, but not in the conclusion. That claim is checked against only two retraining-free methods, Golatkar et al. and SSD. Zero-shot unlearning (Chundawat et al. 2023b) is cited but not contrasted on its label requirements. The statement that output-sensitivity importance 'has not been applied in unlearning' is an absence claim that the paper does not support with a survey. Whether that claim holds was not assessed here. The 'require only' framing also leaves out that importances computed over the full dataset D must be precomputed and stored.
synthesis.likely_impact: Practitioners who must forget data without reliable labels may benefit. The appendix names copyright catalogues and models trained with semi-supervised learning, where pseudo-labels may be untrustworthy. A drop-in, label-free variant of SSD lowers the operational barrier to retraining-free unlearning. Several factors may limit influence. The change is a single-component substitution. Its effectiveness is uneven in subclass settings. Like SSD, it depends on choosing α and λ. Privacy is evaluated only with an entropy-based membership inference attack, which offers limited assurance for regulatory use. The motivating use cases are argued only briefly, and mostly in the appendix.
synthesis.decision_synthesis: In favour: the idea is simple, clearly stated, and practically motivated. It removes the label requirement from a retraining-free method. Full-class results broadly support competitiveness with SSD, and in some cases favour LFSSD; for example, ViT lamp forget accuracy is 0.00 for LFSSD versus 36.89 for SSD. A single LFSSD setting (α=10, λ=1) is used across benchmarks, which may suggest some robustness of the defaults. Against: the headline claim that the approach is 'equally effective as Fisher information' is not uniformly supported. Subclass results diverge in both directions. In ViT mushroom, forget accuracy is 31.42 for LFSSD versus 6.68 for SSD. In ViT baby, LFSSD gives 86.81 against a retrain value of 93.23. No aggregate comparison is given. The questions most likely to change the assessment are: (1) whether the ten repetitions vary anything that affects (LF)SSD. The ±0.00 spreads, together with the description of the method as deterministic, suggest they may not, in which case comparisons with stochastic baselines rest on single-model results; and (2) how the priority claim differs from zero-shot unlearning and other label-free approaches. Non-blocking improvements: explain how hyperparameters were selected, especially the differing SSD (α=50, λ=0.1) and LFSSD (α=10, λ=1) settings in Table 3; hedge the conclusion's priority and 'robust' wording given the acknowledged α sensitivity; and move the practical motivation into the main text.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In Table 6 (RN sea), retrain retains 91.47 Df but LFSSD gives 18.06. Under the paper's own criterion, this is over-forgetting relative to retrain, and here SSD is closer to retrain. Other rows (e.g., ViT MR, where LFSSD gives 31.42 vs retrain 26.57) show mixed results.
points: The claim that the method is 'equally effective as Fisher information' is uneven in subclass unlearning. LFSSD Df deviates substantially from retrain in several cases, so 'equally effective' should be scoped.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors describe the method as an extension of SSD that substitutes the importance estimator from Aljundi et al. Read together, these statements show the originality lies in applying the MAS estimator within SSD to remove the label requirement. That is a modest but clearly delimited advance, which fits a Tiny Paper.
points: LFSSD is positioned by the authors as an extension of their own SSD, swapping Fisher importance for the MAS-style output-sensitivity importance. The novelty is a targeted combination of two existing components rather than a new mechanism.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: The cost parity and the label-free scenarios described in the appendix support practical relevance.
points: Removing label and retain-set storage needs is practically motivated, and the method's cost matches SSD's.

originality.reasoning: The conclusion drops the hedge. The paper does not explain how the cited zero-shot and retraining-free methods (e.g., FisherForgetting) differ on label requirements. Chundawat et al. 2023b ('Zero-shot machine unlearning') is grouped with retraining-based methods but is never distinguished explicitly. Whether the primacy claim holds depends on how the paper characterises that method's label requirements.
points: The 'first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples' claim is hedged in the introduction. The conclusion restates it without the hedge, and the paper cites zero-shot unlearning (Chundawat et al. 2023b) without distinguishing it.
The 'first' primacy claim depends on a 'retraining-free' qualifier, but the paper does not discuss the cited zero-shot unlearning work. That work may also avoid needing labelled retain data.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: The scenarios the authors name point to concrete practitioner audiences who are likely to build on this work.
points: Label-free, retraining-free unlearning has plausible practical uses that the paper names: copyrighted data catalogues and semi-supervised models.

originality.reasoning: The authors' own positioning credits the importance measure to Aljundi et al. and the dampening framework to SSD. Originality rests on the transfer and on the label-free property. The claim of non-application in unlearning is author-reported and was not verified here.
points: The authors frame the work as a 'novel extension' of their own SSD that borrows importance estimation from continual learning (Aljundi et al.). The novelty is therefore a combination and transfer of two existing ideas, not a new importance measure.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: Table 1 shows LFSSD Df=0 on both architectures, while SSD fails on ViT. On CIFAR100 lamp, LFSSD reaches 0.00 Df accuracy and keeps Dr near the baseline for both ResNet18 and ViT. On ViT it outperforms SSD (Df 0.00 vs 36.89). This directly substantiates the competitiveness claim for full-class forgetting.
points: In full-class unlearning, LFSSD matches or exceeds SSD in retaining Dr accuracy while driving Df to 0. On ViT lamp, SSD leaves 36.89% Df while LFSSD reaches 0.00.
The tables support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD and retraining baselines on full-class forgetting. Subclass results are mixed.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In ViT subclass MR, LFSSD leaves Df at 31.42 versus 6.68 for SSD. Both methods are deterministic, so each configuration is a single result. No aggregate comparison is given. In the ViT subclass rows, LFSSD's Df differs from SSD's in both directions, and both differ from retrain. 'Equally effective' is therefore not uniformly supported. In the ViT subclass rows, LFSSD's Df accuracy exceeds SSD's in some cases. The quoted MR row shows 31.42 for LFSSD versus 6.68 for SSD. The table also uses per-task α values. Together this suggests the method is comparable on average rather than equivalent in every setting. In Table 1, ViT lamp forget-set accuracy is 0.00 for LFSSD versus 36.89 for SSD. LFSSD retain-set accuracy (76.36 and 89.03) is close to the baseline. Using a single α per task argues against per-class tuning.
points: The tables broadly support 'competitive with SSD' on class unlearning. They do not uniformly support 'equally effective as Fisher information', because subclass results are mixed.
The tables broadly support 'competitive with SSD' for full-class unlearning. Results are mixed for subclass unlearning, which undercuts the claim of being 'equally effective'.

The tables broadly support LFSSD being competitive with SSD. However, the claim that it is 'equally effective as Fisher information' is not uniform across settings: ViT subclass Df is high for several classes.

Across the class-unlearning tables, LFSSD reaches 0 forget-set accuracy while keeping retain-set accuracy near the baseline. In several settings it avoids SSD failures, and it uses one fixed α per task.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors credit both parts of the method to prior work: the dampening rule comes from SSD and the importance estimator comes from Aljundi et al. The original element is combining them so that unlearning needs no labels. This is honest framing of an incremental but useful idea, and it suits a tiny-paper format. The authors credit the estimator to prior work and claim only its application to unlearning. Whether that application is in fact unprecedented has not been verified here.
points: LFSSD is positioned as an extension of SSD that swaps Fisher-based importance for the output-sensitivity importance of Aljundi et al. (2018). The novelty is a targeted, clearly stated substitution rather than a new algorithm.
The novelty lies in transferring an existing estimator, which the authors attribute to Aljundi et al. (2018), into SSD. The importance measure itself is not new, and the authors acknowledge this.

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: Two features drive adoption: the method removes the label requirement, and it keeps SSD's cost. The motivating scenarios are plausible, though the authors argue them rather than demonstrate them.
points: Label-free, retraining-free unlearning addresses practical settings such as copyright catalogues and semi-supervised models. Practitioners and unlearning researchers could readily adopt it as a drop-in replacement for SSD's importance step.

originality.reasoning: The priority claim is checked against only two retraining-free methods, both described as Fisher- and label-based. The related-work coverage is too narrow to fully support a 'first' claim. The paper groups Chundawat 2023b (which it cites as 'Zero-shot machine unlearning') with the retraining-based methods. It never states that method's label requirements, so the distinction behind the priority claim is not made explicit. The introduction hedges the claim, but the conclusion drops the hedge. The phrase 'require only' also omits the precomputed importances over D, which must be stored.
points: The 'first retraining-free unlearning method to require only the unlabelled forget samples' claim is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. However, the related work cites only one other retraining-free method, Golatkar et al.

The 'first label-free, retraining-free' claim is hedged, but it rests on a short related-work paragraph. The paper itself cites zero-shot unlearning (Chundawat 2023b) without explaining how its own label requirement differs.

The claim to be the 'first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples' is hedged in the introduction but unhedged in the conclusion. The method also still relies on importances computed over the full dataset D.

originality.reasoning: Both building blocks are attributed to prior work. The claim that this importance measure has 'not been applied in unlearning' is the authors' own view and was not verified here. The authors explicitly credit Aljundi et al. for the estimator. The original contribution is therefore its transfer into the SSD unlearning pipeline.
points: The authors present the work as a 'novel extension' of SSD that imports MAS importance from continual learning. The novelty is a combination of existing components, and both sources are attributed.

The authors frame LFSSD as an extension of their own SSD, using a sensitivity measure borrowed from Aljundi et al. (2018). Novelty rests on combining the two for unlearning, not on a new importance measure.
